meta.blurb: Two and a half thousand years ago a teacher in China spoke simply about learning, kindness, honesty and how to live well. His students wrote his words down. Meet Confucius through the sayings and small stories of the Analects.
meta.bible: The Analects: a book of 20 short books of sayings and conversations of Confucius and his students, collected by his followers after his death; the Chinese title Lunyu means Selected Sayings. Confucius: the teacher, also called Kongzi or Master Kong and called the Master by his students; he lived from about 551 BC to about 479 BC. Lu: the small state in China where he was born. Qi, Wei, Chen: other states where he travelled. Yan Hui: his favourite student, also called Yan Yuan, poor and joyful, who died young. Zilu: a brave, quick student, also called Ji Lu. Zigong: a clever, eloquent student. Zengzi: a thoughtful student. Ran Qiu: a student, sometimes called Ran You. Zai Wo: a student who slept in the day. Zhonggong: a student who asked about humaneness. You Ruo: a student. Gongxi Hua: a student who asked why. Ji Kangzi: a powerful minister of Lu. Duke Jing: the ruler of Qi. The Duke of Wei: the ruler of Wei. Yao and Shun: legendary sage-kings of ancient China. The gentleman: a person of good character; the word means the noble person; the small person is someone who thinks only of his own gain. Humaneness: goodness toward others, called ren in Chinese; it is the quality that Confucius valued most. Ritual: the courteous forms of good conduct, called li. The Way: the right path of living and ruling. Heaven: the higher power that Confucius spoke of with respect. Voice and tone: calm, clear, warm and respectful; each beat names the book of the Analects it comes from; everything is attributed to Confucius or his students and nothing is invented; there is no preaching.

B1B2: Confucius was a teacher who lived in China about 2,500 years ago. His students and their students collected his sayings in a book called the Analects.
The first book of the Analects begins with a gentle question from Confucius. He asks whether it is not a pleasure to learn something and then to practise it again and again.

The third question asks whether someone is not a true gentleman if he stays calm when others do not know his worth. Later in the same book, Confucius adds that we should worry less about being unknown and more about not knowing other people.

One of his students, Zengzi, said that he examined himself on three points every day. He asked whether he had been honest when helping others, true to his friends, and faithful to what he had been taught.
A student named You Ruo said that a person who respects his family will rarely cause trouble outside it. Goodness is like a tree, he said, and respect at home is its root.
In the second book, Confucius says that a ruler who leads by good character is like the Pole Star. It stays in its place, and all the other stars turn toward it.

Confucius said that if rulers use only laws and punishments, people will try to avoid the punishment but will feel no shame. If rulers lead by good example, people will feel shame and correct themselves.
Confucius told his students that studying without thinking is a waste of effort. Thinking without studying, he warned, is dangerous, because a mind can wander far from the truth.
Confucius once said to his student Zilu, who was bold and eager, that he would teach him what knowledge is. When you know something, say that you know it, and when you do not, admit that you do not.
Confucius also said that to see what is right and not to do it shows a lack of courage. Knowing the good is not enough, he believed, unless we act on it.

In the fourth book, Confucius says that the gentleman understands what is right, while the small person understands only what is profitable. The question, then, is which of these two we ask first when we make a choice.

Confucius said that when we see a worthy person, we should think about how to become their equal. When we see someone who is not worthy, we should look inside ourselves and ask whether we have the same fault.
The gentleman wants to be slow to speak but quick to act. He thought words should be chosen with care, because it is shameful when our actions fall short of them.
Confucius said that virtue is never lonely, because it always has neighbours. People who live well tend to attract others who want to live well too.

In the fifth book, a student named Zai Wo slept through the day, and Confucius said that rotten wood cannot be carved. He added that he used to trust people's words, but now he also watches what they do.

Zilu wished to share his carriage and clothes with friends, and Yan Yuan wished never to boast of his good deeds. Asked for his own wish, Confucius hoped to comfort the old, be trusted by friends, and care for the young.
Yan Hui, whom Confucius admired most, lived in a narrow lane with only a bowl of rice and a cup of water. Other people would have found such a life miserable, but Yan Hui never lost his joy.
Confucius said that knowing something is not as good as loving it. And loving it is not as good as taking real delight in it.
Zigong asked whether a person who helps all the people would be called humane. He said that such a person would be a sage, and that the humane person, wanting to succeed, helps others succeed too.
Confucius said that he passed on old wisdom and did not invent new ideas. He trusted the teachings of the ancient sages and loved them, and he wanted to hand them on.
Confucius said that he would only teach those who were eager to learn. If he showed a student one corner of a square and the student could not find the other three, he would stop.
Confucius said that he could eat plain rice, drink water, and sleep with his arm for a pillow, and still be happy. Wealth and honour won in the wrong way, he said, were like floating clouds to him.

Confucius said that when three people walk together, he is sure to find a teacher among them. He would copy the good qualities of one person and correct the same faults in himself when he saw them in another.
The seventh book also gives us a short portrait of Confucius himself, written by his students. He was warm but strict, dignified but never harsh, and respectful and relaxed at the same time.
Zengzi said that a scholar must be broad-minded and strong, because his burden is heavy and his road is long. His burden is humaneness, and the road does not end until he dies.
Standing by a river, Confucius said that everything passes like this, never stopping by day or by night. Many readers have heard in his words a gentle reminder that time does not wait.
Confucius said that a great army can lose its commander by force. But not even the strongest power can take away the will of an ordinary man.
The tenth book describes how Confucius behaved in daily life, in great matters and small. When a stable burned down, he asked only whether anyone was hurt, and not about the horses.
Zilu asked how one should serve the spirits of the dead. Confucius replied that we should first learn to serve living people, and first understand life before death.
Zilu asked whether he should act as soon as he heard a good idea, and Confucius told him to wait. When Ran Qiu asked the same question, Confucius told him to act at once.
When Yan Hui died early, Confucius cried out that Heaven had destroyed him. His students said that he grieved too much, but Confucius asked, for whom, if not for this man, should he grieve?

Yan Yuan asked Confucius what humaneness is, and the teacher said that it means mastering oneself and following good conduct. It is a matter of one's own effort, he added, and not something that depends on others.
In the same book, Confucius told his student Zhonggong not to do to others what he would not want done to himself. When he went out, he should behave as if he were meeting an honoured guest.
Zigong asked Confucius what a good government needs most in order to stand firm. He said that it needs food, weapons and trust, and that trust is the last thing it can give up.
Duke Jing of the state of Qi asked Confucius for his advice about government. He said that everyone must truly be what he is: a ruler, a minister, a father, a son.

A powerful minister asked whether he should punish wrongdoers to help the people follow the Way. Confucius replied that the ruler's character is the wind and the people are the grass, which bends when the wind blows.
Zilu asked what Confucius would do first if a ruler asked him to govern a state. He said he would put names right, because when names are wrong, words fail and nothing gets done.
On a journey to the state of Wei, Confucius saw how many people lived there. Ran Qiu asked what should be done for them, and Confucius said that they should first be made prosperous, then taught.
Confucius said that the gentleman seeks harmony without demanding that everyone think alike. The small person demands that everyone agree, but cannot live in harmony.
Confucius said that in ancient times people studied to improve themselves. In his own day, he said, people mostly studied in order to impress other people.

Someone once asked Confucius whether it is right to answer bad treatment with kindness. He answered that then we would have nothing to repay kindness with, so we should repay harm with fairness and kindness with kindness.

Once, in the state of Chen, Confucius and his followers ran out of food, and the students were too weak to stand. Angry Zilu asked whether a gentleman must suffer like this, and Confucius said that a gentleman stays firm in hardship.
Confucius said that a craftsman who wants to do good work must first sharpen his tools. He also warns that those who ignore the distant future will soon have trouble close at hand.
Confucius said that to make a mistake and not correct it is the true mistake. Everyone makes errors, but the wise person looks at his own and mends them.

In the sixteenth book, Confucius names three kinds of friends who help us: the upright, the trustworthy and the well-informed. He names three kinds who harm us: flatterers, pleasers and smooth talkers.
In the seventeenth book, Confucius says that people are close to one another by nature, but far apart through habit and practice. What matters most, then, is the way we choose to live each day.

In the eighteenth book, two farmers told Zilu that the world could not be changed and that his teacher should withdraw from it. Confucius sighed and said that he could not live with birds and beasts, so he must stay among people.

Later, a man told people that Zigong was wiser than Confucius, but Zigong answered that his own wall reached only the shoulder. His teacher's wall, he said, was far higher, and Confucius was like the sun and moon, which no one can climb.
Looking back, Confucius said that he set his heart on learning at fifteen and stood firm at thirty. At seventy, he said, he could follow his heart's desire without ever going wrong.
The last book ends with three things that Confucius said a person must understand: destiny, ritual and words. Without understanding words, he said, we can never really understand other people.
C1C2: Confucius, born about 551 BC in the small state of Lu, became the most famous teacher in the history of China, though in his own lifetime he held little power. He did not write the book himself, for his students and their followers collected his words over many years into twenty short books called the Analects. Reading it is like listening to conversations between a teacher and the people who came to him to learn.

The Analects opens, in its first book, with three small questions, and the first two are gentle. Is it not a pleasure, Confucius asks, to learn something and then put it into practice at the right time? And is it not a joy to have a friend come from far away to visit you?

The third question is the hardest of the three: is a person not a true gentleman if he feels no resentment when other people fail to recognise his worth? Confucius returns to this idea later in the same book, telling his students not to be troubled that no one knows them. Their real concern, he says, should be that they do not yet know other people.

Among the voices in the first book is that of Zengzi, one of the younger students, who said that every day he examined himself on three points. Had he been loyal when planning on behalf of others, and had he been trustworthy in his dealings with friends? Last, he asked, had he actually put into practice everything that his teacher had passed on to him?

Another voice in the first book belongs to You Ruo, one of the students, who observed that a person who is respectful toward parents and elders is seldom inclined to defy those in authority. A wise person attends to the root, he said, for once the root is firm, the Way will grow. Respect within the family is the root of humaneness, the quality that Confucius valued above all.

The second book turns to government, and it begins with a picture that is easy to remember. A ruler who governs through moral character, Confucius says, is like the Pole Star, which stays in its place while all the other stars bow toward it. Real authority, the image suggests, does not push or shout; it simply draws others in by being steady and good.

Rule by orders and punishments, Confucius warned, produces people who learn only to avoid the penalty, and who feel no shame about the wrong itself. Lead them instead by example and by courtesy, and they will develop a sense of shame and, of their own accord, set themselves right. His faith was in the power of character to change a community from the inside, which no threat could ever do from the outside.

Learning and thinking, Confucius taught, are two legs of the same walker, and a person who relies on only one will not travel far. A student who reads everything but never reflects ends with a head full of words and no understanding, while one who reflects without reading must build everything on his own guesses. Walking only one of these roads, he warned, leads either to wasted effort or to real danger.

In the second book Confucius turns to Zilu, a brave, impulsive student who liked to answer first and think later, and offers to teach him what knowledge really is. When you know a thing, he says, accept that you know it, and when you do not know it, accept that you do not. This honest line between what we know and what we merely suppose, he explains, is the beginning of true knowledge.

To see what is right and fail to do it, the second book declares, is a lack of courage. Confucius had no patience for people who admired goodness from a safe distance, praising it in conversation and avoiding it in practice. For him, understanding and action belonged together, and a good intention that never became a deed was only half a virtue.

The fourth book is full of short, sharp contrasts, and one of the best known sets two kinds of people side by side. The gentleman, Confucius says, understands what is right, while the small-minded person understands only what is profitable. The difference is not one of rank or wealth but of the question each person asks first when a choice has to be made.

Other people, in the fourth book, become a kind of mirror in which we may study our own character. When we meet someone admirable, Confucius says, we should think of how to become his equal, and when we meet someone who is not, we should turn our eyes inward and ask whether we share the fault. In this way every person we meet, good or bad, has something to teach us.

The same book praises a quiet kind of strength, the kind that does not need to announce itself. The gentleman, Confucius says, wishes to be slow in his speech but quick in his actions. For people of old were careful with their words, he explains, because they were ashamed to think that their deeds might fall short of them.

There is comfort in one short saying from the fourth book: virtue, Confucius says, is never alone, for it always has neighbours. A person who tries to live well may at times feel isolated, yet goodness has a way of drawing others to it, as a lit window draws travellers across a dark field. In time, those who strive for the good find that they are in good company.

The fifth book shows that the Master could be sharp with his students. When Zai Wo was found sleeping during the day, Confucius remarked that rotten wood cannot be carved and a crumbling wall cannot be plastered, and he asked why he should bother to scold him at all. He then added a lesson for himself: once he had trusted that people would act as they spoke, but now he listened to their words and also watched their deeds.

On one occasion, as the fifth book tells it, Confucius asked two students to say what each of them most wished for. Zilu answered that he would like to share his carriage, his horses and his fine clothes with his friends, and not mind if they wore them out, while Yan Yuan hoped never to boast of his own goodness or make a show of his merits. When they turned the question back to the teacher, he said simply that he wished to give peace to the old, to be trusted by his friends, and to care tenderly for the young.

In the sixth book, Confucius pauses to admire Yan Hui, the student he valued above all others. How admirable he was, the teacher says, living in a narrow lane on a bamboo bowl of rice and a gourd of water, a hardship that most people could not have borne without misery. Yet through all of it, Hui's cheerfulness never changed, for his happiness did not depend on what he owned.

There are three steps on the road of learning, Confucius says in the sixth book, and each is higher than the one before. To know a subject is good, but those who know are surpassed by those who love it, and those who love it are surpassed in turn by those who take delight in it. The student who has reached delight no longer feels study as a duty, because it has become one of life's pleasures.

Zigong, the eloquent student, once asked what Confucius would say of a person who could bring benefit to all the people and help everyone around him: could he be called humane? Such a person, the teacher replied, would be far more than humane, a sage, for even the legendary kings Yao and Shun would have found it hard to do so much. The humane person, he added, simply helps others to stand firm and to succeed, wishing for them what he wishes for himself.

The seventh book, which is full of the teacher's own character, opens with a modest claim: Confucius says that he passes on what he has received and does not invent, since he trusts the ancient ways and loves them. This humility is a clue to his whole mission, because he saw himself not as the inventor of a new philosophy but as the keeper of a wisdom that the sages of the past had already found. It is a rare thing for a great teacher to insist that his greatest gift is to hand something on.

As a teacher, Confucius was generous with his time, but he was not willing to do his students' thinking for them. He would not open the way for a student who was not eager, he said, and he would not help one who was not struggling to put his own thoughts into words. If he held up one corner of a subject and the student could not come back with the other three, he would not go over it again.

Happiness, as the seventh book describes it, does not depend on comfort or on the opinion of others. Confucius says that there is joy to be found in eating coarse rice, drinking plain water and using a bent arm for a pillow, whereas riches and honours gained by wrong means are to him like clouds drifting past. The one is solid and lasting, the other a vapour that will soon be gone.

Among the seventh book's best-loved sayings is the observation that whenever three people are walking together, Confucius is certain to find a teacher among them. From the good qualities of one he learns what to copy, and from the faults of another he learns what to correct in himself. No one, in other words, is without something to teach, for a clear-eyed learner makes a lesson even of a stranger's mistake.

The students who gathered these sayings sometimes stopped to describe their teacher, and the seventh book gives us a brief portrait. The Master, they say, was gentle yet stern, dignified without being fierce, and respectful while remaining perfectly at ease. It is the picture of a person who has made his character so much his own that opposite qualities sit together in him without strain.

In the eighth book, Zengzi describes what it means to take the path of learning seriously. A scholar must be broad in mind and firm in purpose, he says, for the burden is heavy and the road is long. His burden is humaneness, which is heavy indeed, and the road ends only with death, which is long indeed.

One of the most quoted moments in the ninth book is a single glance at a river. Standing beside the flowing water, Confucius said that everything passes on in just this way, never pausing, day or night. The sentence is short and says little directly, yet generations of readers have heard in it a meditation on time, on change and on the urgency of using our days well.

In the ninth book Confucius makes a claim about the dignity of every human being. The commander of even a great army, he says, can be carried off by force, yet no power on earth can take the will of a single ordinary person. Strength, in this view, lies not in numbers or weapons but in the firmness of a purpose that no one else can seize.

The tenth book is less a collection of sayings than a portrait of how Confucius behaved in his daily life, from the way he dressed to the way he spoke at court. One of its small stories tells of a morning when his stable burned down while he was away at court. Returning, he asked whether anyone had been hurt, and he did not ask about the horses, as if the answer to the first question was the only one that mattered.

In the eleventh book Zilu, always eager for answers, asked Confucius how one ought to serve the spirits, and then asked what he thought about death. The teacher answered with two questions of his own: if a person is not yet able to serve other people, how can he serve the spirits, and if he does not yet understand life, how can he understand death? His replies turn the student back toward the work that lies in front of him, and they show how firmly the Master kept his attention on this world.

The eleventh book also shows how carefully Confucius fitted his advice to each student, for Zilu and Ran Qiu both asked whether they should act at once on what they heard. To Zilu he said wait, and to Ran Qiu he said go, and when a puzzled student asked why, he replied that one was hesitant and the other had the energy of two. A good teacher, this story shows, does not repeat the same advice to everyone but looks closely at the person who is asking.

The eleventh book also holds one of the saddest moments in the Analects, the death of Yan Hui, the student whom Confucius loved best. The old teacher cried out that Heaven had destroyed him, and he wept so bitterly that his followers told him he was grieving too much. Was that so, he asked, and for whom should he grieve, if not for such a man?

The twelfth book is crowded with questions about humaneness, and the best-known of them comes from Yan Yuan, who asked what it really means. To overcome oneself and return to the ritual forms of good conduct, Confucius answered, is humaneness, and if for a single day a person could do this, everyone under heaven would turn toward humaneness. It starts with oneself, he added, and Yan Yuan answered humbly that although he was not quick, he would try to put the lesson into practice.

Zhonggong, another of the students, asked about humaneness too, and the answer he received has become one of the best-known sayings of Confucius. He told him that, on going out, he should behave as though he were receiving an honoured guest, and that he should not impose on others what he would not wish for himself. Then there would be no resentment against him, whether in the state or in his own family.

Zigong asked what a government needs in order to stand, and Confucius named three things: enough food, enough weapons and the trust of the people. If one had to be given up, Zigong pressed, the teacher said it should be the weapons, and if a second had to go, the food. Death comes to all, he reasoned, but a people who no longer trust their rulers have nothing left to stand on.

Duke Jing of the state of Qi once asked Confucius about government, and the answer is one of the shortest in the book. Let the ruler be a ruler, the teacher said, the minister a minister, the father a father and the son a son, which is to say that each person must live up to the duties of his own place. The Duke agreed warmly, saying that if the ruler failed to be a ruler and the son failed to be a son, then even with plenty of grain he could not be sure of eating it.

Ji Kangzi, a powerful minister of Lu, once asked whether he should put the wicked to death in order to bring the people closer to the Way. Why use killing in government, Confucius answered, since if the minister himself desired goodness, the people would be good. The character of a gentleman is like the wind, he said, and the character of ordinary people is like the grass, and when the wind blows over the grass, the grass is sure to bend.

In the thirteenth book Zilu asked what Confucius would do first if the Duke of Wei invited him to run the government. He would begin, the teacher answered, by putting names right, and Zilu, who thought this a long way from practical politics, protested that the Master was being unrealistic. Confucius replied that when names are wrong, speech does not make sense, and when speech does not make sense, nothing can be properly done.

As Ran Qiu drove his teacher's carriage into the state of Wei, Confucius remarked on how numerous the people were. When Ran Qiu asked what should be done for such a population, the answer was to make them prosperous, and when he asked what should come after that, the answer was to teach them. The order is revealing: a hungry person cannot be expected to study virtue, but a prosperous people left without education will not remain good for long.

Harmony is not the same as agreement, according to the thirteenth book. The gentleman, Confucius says, seeks harmony without insisting on sameness, while the small person insists on sameness and yet never achieves harmony. A choir, one might say, achieves its beauty through many different voices working together, not through one voice repeated.

The fourteenth book contains a complaint about learning that will sound very familiar today. In ancient times, Confucius says, people studied for the sake of improving themselves, whereas in his own day they study in order to impress other people. The test of learning, he implies, is what it does to the learner, not how it looks to an audience.

Someone once asked Confucius what he thought of repaying injury with kindness, and the teacher answered with a question of his own: with what, then, would one repay kindness? Repay injury with uprightness, he said, and repay kindness with kindness. The saying draws a sober line between justice and generosity, for to treat the kind and the cruel in exactly the same way would be to make no difference between them at all.

The fifteenth book remembers a hard time in the state of Chen, when the supplies ran out and the followers of Confucius grew so weak that none of them could rise. Zilu, his temper roused, came to the teacher and demanded to know whether even a gentleman had to suffer such hardship. Confucius replied that a gentleman certainly does, but that he holds firm in want, whereas the small person who is in want loses all restraint.

Preparation is the subject of two short sayings in the fifteenth book. A craftsman who wishes to do his work well, Confucius says, must first sharpen his tools, and he gave this advice to a student who had asked how to live a humane life. He adds a warning to the same effect: anyone who does not think about what lies far ahead will find sorrow waiting close at hand.

A short line in the fifteenth book contains a whole philosophy of self-improvement and honesty. To have a fault and not to correct it, Confucius says, is what we should truly call a fault. Everyone goes wrong at some time, but the person who sees his error and sets it right has turned a failure into a lesson, while the one who defends his error only makes it grow.

The sixteenth book is built largely on lists, and one of them concerns friendship. Three kinds of friends are beneficial, Confucius says: the upright, the trustworthy, and the well-informed. Three are harmful: those who flatter, those who are ingratiating, and those who talk smoothly but have nothing to say.

By nature, Confucius says in the seventeenth book, people are close to one another, but through practice they grow far apart. The sentence is a quiet defence of education, for it implies that no one is born wicked or noble, and that the habits we form day after day shape the people we become. If this is so, then the most important lessons are the ones that we repeat until they become second nature.

In the eighteenth book, two farmers ploughing a muddy field told Zilu that the world could not be changed and that his teacher would do better to withdraw from it. When Zilu reported their words, Confucius sighed and said that a person cannot live among birds and beasts, and that if he did not keep company with other people, there was no one else to keep company with. If the Way already prevailed in the world, he added, he would not be trying to change it.

The nineteenth book gathers the sayings of the students after the Master's death, and it ends by praising him. When someone remarked that Zigong was wiser than Confucius, Zigong answered that his own wall was only shoulder high, so that anyone could look over it, whereas the Master's wall was many fathoms tall, and a person who could not find the gate would never glimpse the splendour inside. Elsewhere he says that others are like hills that can be climbed, but that Confucius is the sun and the moon, which no one can ever surpass.

Back in the second book, Confucius gives a short summary of his own life, and it makes a fitting place to look back. At fifteen, he says, he set his heart on learning, at thirty he took his stand, and at forty he was free from doubts. At fifty he understood the will of Heaven, at sixty his ear was open to the truth, and at seventy he could follow his heart's desire without overstepping what was right.

The Analects closes, in its twentieth book, with a short sentence about three kinds of understanding. Without understanding destiny, Confucius says, a person cannot become a gentleman, without understanding ritual he cannot take his stand, and without understanding words he cannot know other people. For more than two thousand years, readers in China and far beyond it have returned to these plain, thoughtful sayings, finding in a teacher who claimed only to pass on old wisdom a guide for the long road of learning, and of living well.
